blocks.text: Reflection prompting has a model attempt a task, examine real feedback about how that attempt actually went, an error message, a failed test, an unsuccessful outcome, and write an explicit reflection on what went wrong before trying again, informed by that reflection.

This topic covers the attempt, reflect, retry loop, why reflection needs genuine external feedback to be effective, and how it differs from self-critique prompting, covered in the next topic, which reviews a single output without needing that external feedback signal.
1. What Reflection Prompting Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225142-130694412.png

Reflection prompting structures a task as a loop, attempt the task, observe real feedback on how that attempt performed, reflect explicitly on what specifically went wrong, and use that reflection to inform an improved next attempt.
2. The Attempt, Reflect, Retry Loop
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225142-764459491.png

Each cycle through the loop follows the same pattern, a concrete attempt is made, genuine feedback about that attempt result is gathered, the model reflects specifically on why the feedback turned out the way it did, and a revised attempt incorporates that reflection.

code.content:
Attempt 1: [generated code]
Feedback: Test 'test_edge_case' failed with an IndexError.
Reflection: The function does not handle an empty input list, causing the index error.
Attempt 2: [revised code that handles the empty list case]

blocks.text: 3. Reflection Needs Real Feedback to Be Useful

blocks.alt: Reflection Needs Real Feedback to Be Useful
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225143-8514390.png

The reflection step is only as good as the feedback it has to work with, a genuine error message, a specific failed test case, a concrete unsuccessful outcome, gives the model something real to reason about, without that grounded feedback, a reflection risks being vague speculation rather than an actual diagnosis.
4. A Worked Example, Debugging Through Reflection

blocks.alt: A Worked Example, Debugging Through Reflection
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225143-528203878.png

A code generation task fits this pattern especially well, a first attempt at a function gets run against a real test suite, a specific failure gets fed back to the model, the model reflects on the actual cause of that specific failure, and a revised attempt addresses exactly that cause.

blocks.text: 5. Storing Reflections Across Multiple Attempts
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225144-826605718.png

In more advanced implementations, reflections from one task attempt can be stored and referenced during later, related attempts, letting a system accumulate lessons over time rather than starting fresh with no memory of past mistakes on every single new task.

blocks.title: This connects to agent memory concepts covered elsewhere
blocks.content: Storing reflections as persistent memory across attempts is closely related to agent memory systems, covered in more depth in the separate AI Agents and Tool Calling course.

blocks.text: 6. Reflection Prompting vs Self-Critique Prompting
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225144-181165037.png

Reflection prompting specifically relies on real external feedback, a test result, an execution error, an actual measured outcome, across multiple attempts at a task, self-critique prompting, covered in the next topic, instead has the model review its own single output directly, without needing an external feedback signal or multiple attempts, the two techniques are related but structurally distinct.
7. Where Reflection Prompting Works Well
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785473225144-706263934.png

Reflection prompting works especially well for tasks with a genuinely verifiable outcome, code that either passes tests or does not, a calculation that either matches a known answer or does not, tasks lacking any clear, checkable feedback signal give the reflection step much less concrete material to reason from.
8. The Cost, Multiple Attempts and Feedback Loops

Reflection prompting requires running an actual attempt, gathering real feedback, often by executing code or checking a result against ground truth, and then making another model call, this full loop costs meaningfully more time and compute than a single pass attempt, reserved for tasks where that investment pays off in genuinely improved results.
9. When Reflection Prompting Is the Right Tool

Reflection prompting is the right choice specifically for tasks with a genuine, checkable feedback mechanism and where a first attempt commonly falls short in a way that concrete feedback could actually reveal, code generation and debugging are the clearest and most common example.
Worked Example
A developer builds a coding assistant that generates a function to parse a specific file format, the first generated attempt fails on a real test case involving an unusual but valid file structure.

Feeding that specific test failure back to the model, and asking it to reflect on why its current approach does not handle that structure before generating a revised attempt, produces a second version that correctly handles the edge case, demonstrating how grounding the reflection in a real, concrete failure produces a genuinely targeted fix rather than a generic rewrite.
Common Mistakes

items: Asking a model to reflect without providing any real, concrete feedback for it to reason about
Applying reflection prompting to a task with no genuinely verifiable outcome, leaving the reflection step without solid ground to stand on
Confusing reflection prompting, which relies on external feedback across attempts, with self-critique, which reviews one output directly
Not accounting for the added cost and latency of running multiple attempt and feedback cycles

blocks.text: Practice

Take a coding task, generate a first solution, run it against a real test case, and if it fails, write out what a reflection on that specific failure would say, then use that reflection to guide a revised solution.
Key Takeaway

Reflection prompting structures a task as an attempt, real feedback, explicit reflection, and retry loop, working especially well for tasks with a genuinely verifiable outcome like code and tests, and it depends on grounding each reflection in concrete, real feedback rather than vague self-assessment.
